claims.text: The initial feedstock is an equiatomic Ta-Nb-Hf-Ti-Zr hydride blend with oxygen below 0.1 wt%.
Ti powder used as a getter in argon will scavenge oxygen from hydride impurities and atmospheric ingress.
Oxygen scavenging by Ti will prevent alpha-HCP phase formation.

The hydrides decompose in the order TaH0.5, NbH, ZrH2, HfH2, and TiH2, with approximate decomposition temperatures of 300, 400, 500, 600, and 700°C, respectively, according to their formation enthalpies.
The proposed decomposition sequence ensures complete dehydrogenation before alloying.
Sintering in 99.999% argon at 1300°C for 30 minutes is an appropriate consolidation regime.
The Ti getter forms a Ti-O solid solution and TiO2 precipitates that sequester oxygen.
Oxygen sequestration prevents Ti dissolution into the matrix and subsequent alpha-BCC nucleation.
Hydride decomposition releases H2 and the constituent metallic elements.
Formation of stable TiO2 maintains low oxygen activity in the material during sintering.
A water quench from 1300°C at more than 100°C/s will suppress diffusion-controlled transformation and retain a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure.
The rapidly quenched microstructure will have a grain size of 1-5 μm.
Slow cooling will produce a dual-phase alpha-BCC plus beta-BCC microstructure.
The processed alloy will attain density above 98% and oxygen content below 0.05 wt%.
Without a Ti getter, the alloy oxygen content will exceed 0.8 wt%.
Oxygen contents above approximately 0.8 wt% are associated with HfO2 formation and strong hardening.
Elevated oxygen causes alpha-BCC formation.
The no-getter condition will reduce ductility and raise hardness above 500 HV.
The process fails when getter addition is below 5 wt% or quench rate is below 50°C/s.
Absence of alpha-Ti diffraction peaks between 600 and 800°C in the getter-containing sample would confirm successful oxygen scavenging.

contradictions.description: The oxygen-sensitive phase is first identified as alpha-HCP, but later statements describe alpha-BCC nucleation and an alpha-BCC plus beta-BCC microstructure without explaining whether these are the same or different phases.
The hypothesis identifies the unwanted alpha phase as HCP, whereas the experiment calls alpha-Ti BCC. These crystallographic assignments are internally inconsistent.

The material is specified as equiatomic and the boundary excludes non-equimolar compositions, but adding 5-10 wt% Ti powder to the feedstock would make the consolidated alloy Ti-rich if that getter is incorporated rather than physically separated.

The feedstock relies on TiH2-derived Ti as an equiatomic alloy constituent, while the mediator states that oxygen sequestration prevents Ti dissolution into the matrix; the distinction between alloying Ti and separate getter Ti is not defined.
